name: Showing up in AI answers (ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Copilot, Google AI Overviews and AI Mode)
asked_as: why doesn't AI mention our brand
what does ChatGPT say about us
outcome: The owner has a fixed panel of real buying questions with a baseline of who assistants name, how they describe the store and which sources they cite; a ranked change list that fixes what is blocking the store (access, wording, facts, the sources assistants trust); and a monthly read that shows whether it worked, against a control.
first_principles: An AI answer is a summary of the pages the assistant fetched for its own sub-searches. The brand named is the one mentioned most often and most consistently across those sources, not the one with the best single page. So the work is: be readable, use the words the sub-searches use, and be present and correct in the sources that get cited.

Each assistant is its own channel. They search different indexes (Google, Bing, their own), lean on different source types (forums, video, lists, marketplaces, reviews) and pick up changes on different clocks. Measure and plan per assistant.

Measure first. Answers change from run to run and day to day; without a fixed question panel, run the same way each time, any claimed gain is noise. Hold half the questions back as a control when testing what works.

Most AI mentions carry no link, so referral sessions undercount. Read business impact from three places together: AI referral sessions and orders, a how-did-you-hear answer that names AI assistants, and mention share in the panel.

Entity clarity is the cheapest lever: the same name, category, price range, ships-to, returns and key facts on the site, marketplace listings, review profiles, social bios and, where the brand is truly notable, Wikidata. Assistants repeat whichever version they see most, including wrong ones.

No special file or markup is required for Google's AI features; pages must be indexed and snippet-eligible. Structured data helps machines read product facts and feeds shopping surfaces, but it is not a citation lever on its own. llms.txt is unproven: cheap to add, never sold as the fix. Mass AI-written pages spike and then crash.

look_for: Runs where the assistant did not search the web: no citations, answer from training data. Count them apart; they say little about what changes will do this quarter.
Present in one assistant and absent in another: usually an index gap (not in Bing, not in Google) or a source-type gap (that assistant leans on forums or video the store is not in).
The store named but described wrongly (old price, wrong ships-to, a discontinued product): find the cited page carrying the error and fix it at the source, not only on the site.
A rival named while the store is not, with the same 3 to 5 third-party pages cited across questions: that short list is the work queue.
The store's own page cited but its product not named: the page never says plainly who the product is best for, with facts that can be quoted.
Sub-search wording that never appears in the store's titles, H1s or first sentences (use case, budget, skin type, room size, 'for beginners').
Reviews, FAQs or spec tables that load by JavaScript after the page: invisible to most AI crawlers.
robots.txt allows a crawler but the CDN or firewall blocks it; or the search crawler (the one that decides ChatGPT search visibility) is blocked when only training was meant to be.
Fact conflicts across the site, marketplaces and review profiles (two founding years, two return windows, different product names).
Question queries in Search Console where position holds and clicks fall: AI Overviews are answering; the aim there is to be named in the overview, not to win the click back.
Comparison and 'best X for Y' questions with no fair, dated comparison page anywhere on the site.
Changes judged on the wrong clock: some assistants pick up a new page in days, others in weeks.

decisions.ask: Where should the effort go first: your own pages, or the sources assistants cite?

options.label: Own pages: facts page, answer pages, comparisons, product data
options.pro: fully in our control; some assistants pick it up fast
options.con: will not move assistants that mostly cite third-party sources
options.when: the store's own domain is already among cited sources, or nothing on the site answers the questions

options.label: Third-party sources: lists, reviews, forums, video, press
options.pro: moves the head answers where the brand is mentioned across many sources
options.con: slower, needs outreach and samples; cannot be bought without disclosure
options.when: most citations point to third-party pages and rivals are named through them

options.label: Both, split by what the panel shows (my usual pick)
options.pro: works on both halves of the answer
options.when: the panel shows a mix of own and third-party citations

decisions.recommend: Count the cited URLs in the baseline by type. Weight the effort by that share, after access and wrong facts are fixed, which always come first.

decisions.ask: Test changes against a held-back half of the questions, or change everything at once?

options.label: Hold back half as a control
options.con: half the questions wait a cycle
options.when: the panel has 40 or more questions and the owner wants to know which tactics pay

options.label: Change everything at once
options.con: gains and run-to-run noise look the same
options.when: fixing wrong facts or blocked access, where waiting helps nobody

decisions.recommend: Access and fact fixes go everywhere at once. Content and source work goes to the test half first when the panel is large enough.

rules: Baseline before any change; the panel wording, assistants, settings, location and run count stay fixed month to month. New questions go in a separate block.
Never fake reviews, post as a customer, pay for mentions without disclosure, or hide instructions to AI in pages.
Every fact on the facts page and every profile comes from the org context and matches the live policy pages word for word.
Answer pages open with a one or two sentence direct answer, then a facts table with units and sources, and a refresh date; fewer good pages over many thin ones.
Comparisons are fair, sourced and dated, and say where the rival wins.
Rating and review markup only from reviews shown on the page; Organization markup links only to the brand's real profiles; FAQ markup is optional plain help, with no rich result promised.
llms.txt may be added as a low-cost option, never reported as the cause of a gain. Wikipedia: never write the brand's own article; Wikidata only where the brand is notable, with sourced facts.
Each change names the questions it serves and the products behind them, ranked by gross profit.

checks: Mention share counts only runs where the assistant searched the web; no-search runs are reported apart.
Every cited URL in the report opens, and every fact on the facts page matches the live policy pages.
senior_review: Is the panel made of questions buyers really ask, weighted to the products with the most gross profit?
Did we read each assistant on its own, rather than one blended score?
Are access and wrong facts fixed before any content or outreach work?
Could any tactic here be seen as fake, paid without disclosure, or hidden text?
Does the report say what is proven (crawl access, cited sources) and what is not (llms.txt, markup as a citation lever)?
When will each change be read again, on that assistant's clock, and against which control?
